assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Electric field
items.clue: Vector whose x-component is minus the slope of V against x.

items.label: Point charge
items.clue: Source with E = kQ/r²; taking V = 0 at infinity gives V = kQ/r.

items.label: Weight
items.clue: Pull of gravity: about 10⁻²⁹ N on an electron, so negligible here.

items.label: Equipotential
items.clue: What joined conductors form: every part of the surface at the same V.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a battery maintains a potential difference between its terminals?

options.text: Chemical reactions make new charge, which then collects at the two terminals.
A store of charge put in when it was made keeps its terminals charged until used up.
It pushes out a fixed current, and the potential difference follows from that current.
Chemical reactions move positive and negative charge apart, to opposite terminals.

questions.stem: Particles with charges +Q and −Q are fixed a distance d apart. Point M is midway between them. Which statement about the electric potential at M is correct?

options.text: It is zero, although the electric field at M is not zero.
It is not zero, because the electric field at M is not zero.
It is 4kQ/d, twice the potential that +Q alone produces there.
It has no value until a test charge is placed at M.

questions.stem: In a region of space the electric potential depends only on x and is given by V(x) = V₀(x/a)³, where V₀ and a are positive constants. What is the x-component of the electric field at x = a?

In the worked example, the electron left the plates deflected sideways by a distance y. The potential difference across the plates is now doubled, and the electron enters at twice the speed. What is its sideways deflection at exit now?
questions.explanation: y = ½at², with a ∝ |ΔV| (×2) and t = L/v (×½, so t² × ¼). The deflection is 2 × ¼ = ½ of y.

questions.stem: An infinitely long line of charge with uniform linear charge density λ lies along the axis of a closed cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length ℓ. The net electric flux through this surface is Φ₁. The surface is then replaced by a closed coaxial cylinder of radius 3r and length 2ℓ, and the net electric flux through the new surface is Φ₂. What is the ratio Φ₂/Φ₁?
A plastic sphere of radius 0.10 m carries a charge of 4.0 nC spread uniformly through its volume. What is the magnitude of the electric field 0.050 m from its centre? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
Suppose the permittivity of free space were four times its actual value, with the permeability unchanged. What speed would Maxwell's equations then predict for electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Speed = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Four times ε₀ → √4 = 2 times the denominator → half the speed.

questions.stem: A rod of length L carries charge +Q spread uniformly. At a point on the rod's line, a distance x beyond one end, the potential is V(x) = (kQ/L) ln((x + L)/x). What is the magnitude of the electric field at that point?
questions.explanation: E_x = −dV/dx = −(kQ/L)[1/(x + L) − 1/x] = kQ/[x(x + L)]. For x ≫ L it becomes kQ/x², a point charge.

questions.stem: A very long, solid, insulating cylinder of radius R has a uniform positive volume charge density ρ. V_s is the electric potential at the cylinder's surface and V₀ is the electric potential on its axis. What is the potential difference V_s − V₀?
For two points A and B in an electric field, V_B − V_A = −50 V. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A charged object moved from A to B changes U_E by −50 J, whatever its charge
A −1.0 C charge moved from A to B lowers U_E by 50 J, as B is at lower potential
U_E falls by 50 J per coulomb on the straight path, and by more on a longer, curved path
If a +1.0 C charge were moved from A to B, by any path, U_E would change by −50 J

questions.stem: A proton and an alpha particle are placed, one at a time, at the same point in a uniform electric field. The alpha particle has twice the charge of the proton and about four times its mass. Gravity is negligible. What is the ratio (acceleration of the alpha particle) / (acceleration of the proton)?
questions.explanation: Correct. Acceleration = charge × E ÷ mass, so the ratio is (2/4) = 1/2. The alpha particle accelerates half as much.

questions.stem: A very long, solid, insulating cylinder of radius R has a uniform volume charge density. The magnitude of the electric field is E₁ at a distance R/2 from the axis and E₂ at a distance 2R from the axis. What is the ratio E₂/E₁?
